item.title: Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World | Arthouse Now — Tue Nov 3, 7:00 PM — IU Cinema
item.description:
Featuring interviews with her close friends and fans—including John Waters, Stephen Colbert, Lucy Dacus, and Steve Buscemi—this deeply personal portrait considers the poet Mary Oliver's lifetime of work and captures the natural beauty that inspired her. Spend this one evening of your wild and precious life exploring her remarkable life!
Celebrated best-selling poet, Pulitzer Prize-winner, lover of dogs and long walks in the woods, openly queer but intensely private, Mary Oliver was America’s unlikely contemporary mystic, stalking the ponds and forests of Cape Cod for nearly 50 years in order to open herself—and her readers—to the known and unknowable world. From a lonely childhood to literary fame, Oliver’s life was shaped by devotion to nature, paying attention, and the long journey toward learning to love and to be loved. item.title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature — Wed Nov 4 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Wed Nov 4 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Wed Nov 4 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers

item.title: Charles H. Long Memorial Lecture by Anthony Pinn — Thu Nov 5, 6:00 PM — LEE NORVELLE THEATRE AND DRAMA CENTER/MARCELLUS NEAL AND FRANCES MARSHALL BLACK CULTURE CENTER
item.description: Join us in the Neal-Marshall Bridgwaters Lounge on Thursday, November 5 at 6:00PM for the Charles H. Long Memorial Lecture by Anthony Pinn (Agnes Cullen Arnold Distinguished Professor of Humanities at Rice University). "Two Big Problems: Du Bois, African American Literature, and Black Moralism" Reflecting on Robert Paxton's The Anatomy of Fascism, Rob Riemen notes Paxton's claim that fascism is culturally specific; its plasticity allows it to reflect the cultural mood of the times. Therefore, and here is where the point becomes interesting, "fascism in the United States would be religious and anti-black…" This claim brings to mind two questions of human meaning-making posed by W. E. B. DuBois's examination of racialized ontology captured in TheSouls of BlackFolk. The first relates to "freedom" sparked by the Civil War. item.title: Heim Colloquium: "Who owns translations? On Literary Rights and Cultural Ownership" — Fri Nov 6, 9:30 AM — MORRISON HALL
item.description: The Heim Colloquium is made possible by a generous donation to Indiana University by the family of Michael Henry Heim (1943 – 2012), one of the most eminent literary translators of the late twentieth- and early twenty-first century in the US. The Heim bequest allows Indiana University to organize events on themes relevant to the many facets of Michael Henry Heim's work. For our inaugural colloquia, we chose to focus on the imagined reader of literary translations (in 2024) and translator paratexts, the introductions and afterwords translators have written about their work (in 2025). For this year's event, we invited a core group of translation-focused graduate students at IU Bloomington to take the lead in forming the questions to be addressed and inviting a panel of experts to help us address them. The title of this year's colloquium is "Who Owns Translation?" Who owns translations? Is it the translator? The author of the source text? The publisher? The "foundation" and other estate

item.title: Affirmation Friday — Fri Nov 6, 11:00 AM — Indiana Memorial Union – Table 2
item.description:
Affirmation Friday is a tabling event at the Indiana Memorial Union designed to support students’ mental well-being during their first month of the semester. Our organization will hand out positive affirmations to passing students and provide a space for them to write down their thoughts and feelings about their first month of school. The event aims to foster a sense of belonging and encourage students to pause, reflect, and practice self-kindness during a busy and often stressful transition. Participation is free and open to all students, and no sign-up is required. Materials will include affirmation cards, writing supplies, and a table display.
Hosted by: Black Men Evolve
Additional Information can be found at: https://beinvolved.indiana.edu/event/12948047
Source: IU beINvolved Student Orgs

item.title: Megan Fernandes Poetry Reading — Fri Nov 6, 6:00 PM — Morgenstern Bookstore
item.description:
Megan Fernandes is a South Asian American writer living in NYC. She was born in Canada and raised in the Philadelphia area. Her family are East African Goans. Fernandes has work published in The New Yorker, TheAmerican Poetry Review, Tin House, Ploughshares, Chicago Review, Boston Review, Rattle, PANK, The Common, Guernica, the Academy of American Poets, and McSweeney's Internet Tendency, among others. She is the author of The Kingdom and After (Tightrope Books, 2015) and Good Boys (Tin House, 2020). Her third book of poetry, I Do Everything I'm Told (Tin House), was published in summer 2023. Fernandes is an Associate Professor of English and the Writer-in-Residence at Lafayette College where she teaches courses on poetry, creative nonfiction, and critical theory. She holds a PhD in English from the University of California, Santa Barbara and an MFA in poetry from Boston University.
Source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute

item.description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Mon Nov 9 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Mon Nov 9 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. item.description:

Thursday, November 12th| 1-2PM | Hamilton Lugar School GA2134 This presentation explores the recognition and representation of Latin American women artists, considering how their voices and experiences can expand our understanding of the region's artistic histories. Dr. Namorato is an associate professor in the Department of Spanish and Portuguese and co-editor of The Other Fridas: The Lives and Works of Latin American Women Artists.
